title: dynamic-latency-flooring-queue-tempering
author: Asha Patel
release_notes: Introduce dynamic latency-flooring and queue tempering to improve fairness between latency-sensitive and throughput requests; no public API changes. Enable via runtime flag; gradual rollout.
description: Motivation: We continue to see tail-latency regressions for latency-sensitive short requests under mixed workloads where large KV/prefetch-heavy batches dominate steady-state admission. Existing fairshare/admission mechanisms reduced average latency but left a class of short, low-token requests starved during microbursts. This PR implements a lightweight, dynamic 'latency-flooring' layer on top of the continuous batcher that (1) establishes a short-term per-tenant latency floor and (2) tempers large-burst admission to prevent transient starvation. Goals: reduce P99 for latency-sensitive routes by 15-30% in mixed workloads, avoid throughput regressions >5%, be rollback-safe and feature-flagged for staged rollout.

benchmark_summary: With PR:       P50=24ms, P95=62ms, P99=154ms, throughput=1165rps
Tail improvement: P99 down 28% with throughput drop 2.9%
KV-heavy scenario: P99 improved 21% for short requests; long request 99th increased ~3% (within SLA thresholds)
design_notes: Latency-flooring: per-tenant sliding quantile (configurable window 10s) computes target floor (e.g., 95th) and exposes a short-lived credit budget so requests classified as 'latency-sensitive' are admitted preferentially until budget drains.

Queue-tempering: each batcher slot has a 'temperature' that rises when admitted request latency or queue-occupancy exceeds thresholds; higher temperature applies soft backpressure to new large requests by probabilistically delaying admission (exponential decay to cool down).

KV interplay: requests annotate kv-weight (0..1) from kvcache prefetch hints; during high-temperature windows, kv-weighted requests are deprioritized to avoid long prefetch+kernel overheads starving short requests.

Kernel hints: latency-floor requests prefer low-overhead kernels with reduced setup + smaller concurrency to shave per-request overhead; this is a hint-only path — runtime still falls back to full kernels if compatibility mismatch.
Rollout: feature-flagged (runtime) with per-tenant opt-in, start at 5% of traffic then ramp to 100% after monitoring P99/P95 and overall throughput.
Safety: metrics/alerts added for 'floor_budget_exhausted', 'temperature_high', 'kernel_hint_fallback' to catch regressions. Config knobs allow disabling kv-weighting or kernel-hinting independently.

review_comments: Miguel Santos: Can we avoid per-request locking hotspots in the quantile collector? Suggest using per-shard accumulators and periodic merge.
Author (Asha): switched to sharded accumulators with lock-free ring buffer reads in quantiles_collector; added microbench results to PR description.
Lena Cho: Kernel hint path looks promising but could we add stricter telemetry to confirm we don't regress model quality on short sequences?

Oliver Grant: How does this interact with existing SLA fallback policies? If a preferred model is overloaded, will tempering cause extra fallbacks?

Author (Asha): tempering is applied before fallback; if a request is delayed and then meets fallback criteria, fallback proceeds as before. Added e2e test that exercises fallback under high temperature.

ci_checks: Integration Bench: pass (bench harness run, regressions within thresholds)
risk_and_mitigation: Risk: over-prioritizing short requests could reduce overall GPU utilization and throughput.
Mitigation: tempering uses probabilistic admission with decay and a tunable max-impact ratio; rollout starts small and metrics enforce throughput budget.
Risk: kernel_hint path might be incompatible for certain model ops.
Mitigation: hint is advisory; we added robust fallback and telemetry to auto-disable on model-level quality regressions.
